newsitem.title: AZERBAIJAN: Caspian AIOC oil group says output date very tight.
newsitem.headline: Caspian AIOC oil group says output date very tight.

text.p: Officials from an $8 billion consortium of Western oil companies developing Azerbaijan's Caspian Sea reserves said on Thursday they still hoped to meet a "very tight" schedule to begin production by August 28.

"We have never given up on the date of August 28, but it is very tight," John Hollis, first vice-president of the Azerbaijan International Operating Company (AIOC), told a news conference in the Azeri capital Baku.
Hollis said a bad Azeri winter, with high winds and rough seas, had made the target harder to meet.
He said efforts to lay 179 km (111 miles) of pipeline from the Chirag field to a shore storage and pumping facility south of Baku had also been complicated.
"By all accounts, this was the toughest Azeri winter in 25 years," he said.
The 13-member AIOC consortium is led by British Petroleum and Norway's Statoil (Den norske stats oljeselskap).
Hollis said the normal amount of time for the completion of such a project is 30 months from beginning to first production, rather than the 18 months AIOC is trying to meet.
"This is a much larger and expensive job than we ever imagined when we started," he said.
He said the August 28 date held no special significance but that every day of construction cost roughly $500,000. "Time is money. A rainy day costs us 500,000 bucks," he said.

He said wells in the three fields involved in the project are expected to be producing 25,000-30,000 bpd by the end of the year. AIOC wants to increase output to peak levels of 700,000-800,000 bpd by 2007-2010.
AIOC vice-president Gregory Rich said test results on samples of oil extracted at some of the sites had shown it to be of high quality.
"It is almost identical to, if not better than, Brent North Sea crude," he said, referring to the world benchmark crude oil Brent Blend.
Two existing pipelines under repair to Georgia's Supsa Black Sea outlet and Russia's export outlet at Novorossiisk are to carry AIOC's so-called "early oil" to world markets.
AIOC will make its recommendations to Azeri President Haydar Aliyev on the building of a large, strategic pipeline to ship its main output after its board meeting on June 10.
Rich said all three routes under consideration from Baku -- to Turkey's Mediterranean port of Ceyhan, to Georgia's Supsa or to Russia's Novorossiisk -- were economically and technically viable.

He said the Azeri government, which will make the final decision on the planned pipeline's route, would need an additional 18 to 24 months to negotiate practical details, including tax and tariff issues, with the countries involved before one route could emerge as the final option.
"The main thing is that it has to be commercially viable," he said.

The possible routes have been the subject of persistent political speculation and a geopolitical tug-of war for the control they will permit over the flow of a large amount of oil to Western markets. Lucrative transit fees are at stake as well.
"This is a long, long process," Rich said. "It is a very big project."
Azeri leaders have embraced a pipeline through Georgia and Turkey but are less enthusiastic about a Russian route.
Rich said the natural market for AIOC oil would be centred in southern Europe, since Caspian oil conformed to the refinery and ecological standards of that region.
